title: Job 36:17–33
context: Elihu continues. He warns Job that he is preoccupied with judging the wicked and urges him not to let wealth, a bribe, or a desire for death turn him aside. He then turns to God's greatness: God is exalted in power, beyond human teaching or correction, and his years are unsearchable. Elihu begins to describe rain, clouds, thunder, and lightning as displays of God's power. This storm imagery prepares the reader for the LORD's speech out of the whirlwind (38:1), but these are still Elihu's words, not the LORD's.

verses.text: “But you are full of the judgment of the wicked. Judgment and justice take hold of you.
verses.arminianNotes: "But you are full of the judgment of the wicked." Arminian readers see Elihu accusing Job of being caught up in a judgment like that of the wicked, perhaps because of his complaints against God.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that the line can be read in more than one way, either that Job judges as the wicked do or that he faces their judgment. In either case, Elihu thinks Job's stance is dangerous.

verses.text: Don’t let riches entice you to wrath, neither let the great size of a bribe turn you aside.
verses.arminianNotes: "Don’t let riches entice you to wrath." Arminian readers see Elihu warning Job against letting wealth or a bribe turn him aside, perhaps a general caution about what can distort judgment.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that the exact sense of these warnings is debated, since Job has lost his wealth. They read the verse as Elihu's general caution and do not press a precise meaning.

verses.text: Would your wealth sustain you in distress, or all the might of your strength?
verses.arminianNotes: "Would your wealth sustain you in distress, or all the might of your strength?" Arminian readers see Elihu reminding Job that human resources cannot rescue anyone in true distress.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note the point that no wealth or strength can save a person before God. Both traditions treat this as shared ground, apart from any judgment on whether Elihu's warning fits Job.

verses.text: Don’t desire the night, when people are cut off in their place.
verses.arminianNotes: "Don’t desire the night, when people are cut off in their place." Arminian readers read this as Elihu warning Job not to long for death, as Job had done in his earlier laments.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that the meaning of "the night" here is uncertain, though many read it as death or disaster. Elihu urges Job not to seek it.

verses.text: Take heed, don’t regard iniquity; for you have chosen this rather than affliction.
verses.arminianNotes: "Take heed, don’t regard iniquity." Arminian readers see Elihu warning Job that he has chosen iniquity "rather than affliction," meaning complaint rather than humble acceptance.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that Elihu charges Job with turning toward wrong in his response to suffering. This is Elihu's charge; the narrator does not make it.

verses.text: Behold, God is exalted in his power. Who is a teacher like him?
verses.arminianNotes: "Behold, God is exalted in his power. Who is a teacher like him?" Arminian readers see Elihu shifting to praise God as the supreme teacher whose instruction all people need.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that God's greatness as teacher fits Elihu's theme that God instructs through affliction. Both traditions treat God's exalted power and wisdom as shared ground.

verses.text: Who has prescribed his way for him? Or who can say, ‘You have committed unrighteousness’?
verses.arminianNotes: "Who has prescribed his way for him?" Arminian readers see Elihu warning that no one can direct God or charge him with wrong. Job's complaints have come close to that.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note the question, "Or who can say, ‘You have committed unrighteousness’?" God is accountable to no one, a theme the LORD will press in his own way (40:2).

verses.text: “Remember that you magnify his work, about which men have sung.
verses.arminianNotes: "Remember that you magnify his work, about which men have sung." Arminian readers see Elihu calling Job to join in praising God's work rather than questioning it.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that Elihu directs Job toward worship. The call to magnify God's works is something both traditions affirm, whatever one thinks of Elihu's diagnosis of Job.

verses.text: All men have looked on it. Man sees it afar off.
verses.arminianNotes: "All men have looked on it. Man sees it afar off." Arminian readers see God's work in creation as visible to everyone, though only partly understood.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that people see God's work "afar off." God's works are visible, but human understanding of them remains distant and incomplete.

verses.text: Behold, God is great, and we don’t know him. The number of his years is unsearchable.
verses.arminianNotes: "Behold, God is great, and we don’t know him." Arminian readers see Elihu's confession of God's greatness and of human limits: even "The number of his years is unsearchable."
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that God's eternity is beyond measure. They compare Job 11:7, where Zophar asks, "Can you fathom the mystery of God?" Both traditions treat God's incomprehensibility as shared ground.

verses.text: For he draws up the drops of water, which distill in rain from his vapor,
verses.arminianNotes: "For he draws up the drops of water." Arminian readers see Elihu turning to rain as an everyday example of God's power and care, as water rises and returns as rain.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that Elihu's description of the water cycle shows God governing ordinary weather. Providence is at work in the most common events.

verses.text: which the skies pour down and which drop on man abundantly.
verses.arminianNotes: Elihu speaks of rain "which the skies pour down and which drop on man abundantly." Arminian readers see rain as a gift poured out generously on people.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note the abundance of God's provision through rain. Both traditions treat God's provision in creation as shared ground, apart from the dispute over Job's suffering.

verses.text: Indeed, can anyone understand the spreading of the clouds and the thunderings of his pavilion?
verses.arminianNotes: "Indeed, can anyone understand the spreading of the clouds." Arminian readers see Elihu stressing that no one fully understands the clouds or "the thunderings of his pavilion."
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note how this question anticipates the LORD's own questions in chapter 38. Elihu's speech begins to point toward the storm from which God will speak.

verses.text: Behold, he spreads his light around him. He covers the bottom of the sea.
verses.arminianNotes: "Behold, he spreads his light around him." Arminian readers see God surrounded by light and ruling even the depths, since he "covers the bottom of the sea."
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note the contrast between light above and the depths below. God's rule extends over the whole of creation, from sky to sea floor.

verses.text: For by these he judges the people. He gives food in abundance.
verses.arminianNotes: "For by these he judges the people. He gives food in abundance." Arminian readers see weather serving two purposes in Elihu's view: judgment and provision.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that the same storms can bring judgment or abundance. This prepares for 37:13, where Elihu says God sends the clouds for correction, for his land, or for loving kindness.

verses.text: He covers his hands with the lightning, and commands it to strike the mark.
verses.arminianNotes: "He covers his hands with the lightning." Arminian readers see a vivid picture of God directing lightning like a weapon. He "commands it to strike the mark," and it goes where he sends it.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that lightning goes where God commands. Later the LORD himself will ask Job, "Can you send out lightnings, that they may go?" (38:35).

verses.text: Its noise tells about him, and the livestock also, concerning the storm that comes up.
verses.arminianNotes: "Its noise tells about him." Arminian readers see the thunder announcing God's approach, and even the livestock sensing "the storm that comes up."
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that the storm is now rising. Elihu's words are building toward the whirlwind from which the LORD will answer Job in 38:1, though Elihu himself is not that answer.
